definition: In computer vision and image processing, Otsu's method, named after Nobuyuki Otsu (大津展之, Ōtsu Nobuyuki), is used to perform automatic image thresholding.
details: In the simplest form, the algorithm returns a single intensity threshold that separate pixels into two classes – foreground and background. This threshold is determined by minimizing intra-class intensity variance, or equivalently, by maximizing inter-class variance. Otsu's method is a one-dimensional discrete analogue of Fisher's discriminant analysis, is related to Jenks optimization method, and is equivalent to a globally optimal k-means performed on the intensity histogram. The extension to multi-level thresholding was described in the original paper, and computationally efficient implementations have since been proposed.
story: Imagine an art restorer who can spot a single cracked tile in a vast mosaic. What your eyes do without thinking, the machine does one careful layer at a time. The machine learns to see the way we do — starting with shapes and edges, then building up to whole objects and faces. The model looks the way you look at a crowd and finds the one face you know. That pixel-to-meaning climb is Otsu's method.
